summary.text: The solar cycle is the roughly 11-year rise and fall in the Sun's activity, measured by how many sunspots appear on its surface.
Across each cycle, sunspots, solar flares, radiation and ejected solar material all swing together from a minimum to a maximum and back again.
The Sun's magnetic field flips near each maximum, so it takes two cycles, about 22 years, for the field to return to its original state.

items.prompt: The Sun's magnetic field reverses once in every 11-year cycle. How long until it points the original way again, polarity included?

items.explain: One flip per cycle means two cycles, about 22 years, are needed to return to the starting state, which is called a Hale cycle.

items.explain: The field flips during each solar cycle, with the flip occurring when the cycle is near its maximum.

items.prompt: How does the Sun's activity since the 1940s compare with its record over the past 11,400 years?

options.label: It is unusually low for the Sun

items.explain: Activity since the 1940s is exceptional: the Sun was this active only about 10% of the past 11,400 years, last around 9,000 years ago.

items.prompt: The full magnetic cycle lasts 22 years, yet most solar research focuses on the 11-year cycle. Why?

items.explain: Nearly all signs of solar activity are insensitive to magnetic polarity, so the 11-year cycle stays the focus of research.

paragraphs.heading: The Sun's eleven-year rhythm
paragraphs.text: The solar cycle is the Sun's regular rise and fall in activity, lasting about 11 years on average. It is measured by counting the sunspots on the Sun's surface. A cycle runs from one solar minimum, when sunspots are fewest, through a solar maximum, when they are most common, and on to the next minimum. It is also known as the sunspot cycle or the Schwabe cycle.

paragraphs.heading: What rises and falls
paragraphs.text: Many things swing together over a cycle: the Sun's radiation, the amount of material it throws out, the number and size of sunspots, and solar flares and coronal loops. Solar activity creates space weather, which affects technology in space and on the ground as well as Earth's atmosphere. It may also play a part in climate swings lasting centuries or longer. Even so, scientists agree that solar changes play only a small role in today's global climate change, since recent solar variation is far weaker than the push from greenhouse gases.

paragraphs.heading: A magnetic flip
paragraphs.text: The Sun's magnetic field reverses during each cycle, close to the maximum. Only after two cycles, about 22 years, is it back where it started, and this full loop is called the Hale cycle. The two halves usually differ: the 11-year cycles tend to alternate between higher and lower total sunspot numbers. In 1961, Harold and Horace Babcock showed that the Sun's surface is magnetized even away from sunspots, and that this weaker field flips with the same rhythm as the sunspot cycle.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting the pattern
paragraphs.text: People saw signs of the cycle for centuries before it was pinned down. Christian Horrebow, who watched sunspots from Copenhagen between 1761 and 1776, first suggested that the Sun's appearance repeats after a certain number of years. The cycle was clearly identified in 1843, when Samuel Heinrich Schwabe found a regular variation in sunspot numbers after 17 years of watching. In 1852 Rudolf Wolf numbered the cycles, starting the first in February 1755. Wolf also created the Wolf number, a sunspot index still used today.

paragraphs.heading: Not perfectly regular
paragraphs.text: Recorded cycles have lasted anywhere from 9 to 14 years, and their strength varies a lot. From 1645 to 1715 very few sunspots were seen at all, a gap later named the Maunder minimum. Over the long run, though, the cycle looks steady: fossil records suggest it has been stable for at least 700 million years, with a length of about 10.62 years estimated for the Early Permian.

paragraphs.heading: Today's Sun
paragraphs.text: Using carbon-14 and beryllium-10, scientists have rebuilt sunspot numbers for the past 11,400 years. They show that the Sun's activity since the 1940s is exceptional, and the last comparable level was about 9,000 years ago. The current cycle, number 25, began in December 2019. One physics-based forecast expects it to be weak but not insignificant, similar to or a little stronger than cycle 24, and rules out a quiet spell like the Maunder minimum in the next decade.
